passage: Forty minutes before the client call, Jahnavi heard the director thank Rafiq for the new sales dashboard. She had built it over three weekends. Her face went hot and she wanted to stand up and say so in front of everyone. But the call was about to start, so she typed a note to herself instead: the dates, the versions, and the message where Rafiq had asked her for the data. After the call she found Rafiq by the coffee machine. "I'd like to talk about the dashboard. I built it, and I'd like that to be clear." Rafiq looked surprised, then muttered that he had not meant to hide it. Jahnavi said she would send the director a short summary of her work, and asked him to send one too.

qa.q: How many weekends did Jahnavi spend building the dashboard?
qa.a: Jahnavi built it over three weekends.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi want to do when she heard the director thank Rafiq?
qa.a: She wanted to stand up and say so in front of everyone, which shows anger, but she held back because the call was about to start.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi do if Rafiq keeps taking credit?
qa.a: She can keep documenting her work, send the director the summary and, if needed, escalate with facts.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have felt at the coffee machine?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and a little caught out; he muttered that he had not meant to hide it, which may or may not be true.

grounding: A colleague feels used when credit is taken and responds by documenting contributions, speaking to the colleague and preparing to escalate with facts.

In the Thursday review at the design studio in Andheri, Kashish clicked to slide six and said, "So I thought we could bring the store map into the app." It was Urmila's idea, from a sketch she'd shown Kashish over tea on Monday.

The manager loved it. Urmila smiled on the outside and gripped her pen under the table.

At home she typed a long message to the team group: "Just so everyone knows, the map idea was mine." Her thumb hovered over send for a full minute. Then she deleted it.

Instead she found the Monday sketch with its date and the email she'd sent Kashish that evening. On Friday she caught Kashish at the coffee machine. "The map idea came from my sketch. I felt used yesterday. Next time, can we present it as ours?"

Kashish went red. "I didn't think it mattered who said it first."

"It matters to me," Urmila said. "If it happens again, I'll take the dates to Sanjay."

qa.q: When had Urmila shown Kashish the sketch?
qa.a: Urmila had shown Kashish the sketch over tea on Monday.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling during the review, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Urmila felt angry and used; she smiled on the outside but gripped her pen under the table.

qa.q: What went well in the way Urmila handled it?
qa.a: She did not expose Kashish in the group chat; she gathered the dated sketch and email, spoke to Kashish directly, and named a fair next step if it happened again.

qa.q: How might Kashish see the coffee-machine conversation?
qa.a: Kashish seems embarrassed and a little defensive, surprised that credit matters so much, but now clearly knows where Urmila stands.

grounding: Shows a young worker angry that a colleague took credit, who documents the work, speaks to the colleague and plans to escalate with facts if needed.

passage:
"Hansa, got a minute?" Harish said at the printer.

"Sure. Great meeting, right? Sunil loved the survey results."

"He did. But the data cleaning was mine. Three weekends. You said 'I sorted the data' twice."

Hansa laughed a little. "We're a team, Harish. Does it matter who did which bit?"

"It matters when appraisals come round. I'm not trying to embarrass you. I'd just like the next update to say who did what."

"You're making a big deal of nothing."

Harish kept his voice level. "Maybe. I've saved the file history and my emails with the cleaned sheets. I'd rather we fix it between us."

The next week Hansa's update read "survey analysis by Hansa" again. Harish booked ten minutes with Sunil and brought the printed file history.

"Thanks for showing me this," Sunil said, scrolling through it. "I'll correct the record in the monthly note."

qa.q: How many weekends did Harish say the data cleaning took?
qa.a: Harish said it took three weekends.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when Hansa called it "a big deal of nothing", and how did he manage it?
qa.a: Harish was angry and felt dismissed, but he kept his voice level and focused on facts and a fair fix.

qa.q: What was wise about the order of Harish's steps?
qa.a: He kept records, spoke to Hansa privately first, and only took the file history to Sunil when the credit-taking happened again.

qa.q: How does Sunil see the situation once he sees the file history?
qa.a: Sunil treats it as a factual problem to correct and appreciates being shown clear evidence rather than accusations.

grounding: Shows a young worker angry at a colleague taking credit who speaks to the colleague first and then escalates calmly with documented facts.
